## Paper Context (4 Claims)

This paper dissects inference-time action refinement for frozen flow-matching VLAs. The pipeline: draw K action samples from frozen VLA → argmin L2 selection → learned residual correction (CRM, ~327K-param MLP). Key findings:

- **C1 (Decomposition)**: Learned correction is the active mechanism (+5.3pp at K=10, 68% at K=5). Multi-sampling is an enabling condition, not the driver. This contrasts with LLM test-time compute where selection is primary.
- **C2 (Conditioning-Magnitude)**: obs_only features stable (14-18% across all ε), perdof conformal features collapse to 0%. Same architecture, same training, only conditioning differs.
- **C3 (Boundaries)**: Three distribution shifts cause CRM to fail: input shift (K=1, 10.3%), task shift (proximity-dependent: near-OOD adversarial -12pp, far-OOD neutral/positive), feature shift (perdof→0%). Near-OOD more dangerous than far-OOD. Also: tokenized VLAs produce near-identical samples, so pipeline requires stochastic diversity.
- **C4 (Adaptive K)**: K=2 L2 pairwise distance as uncertainty probe (ρ=0.9979 vs K=10 variance). Dynamically allocate compute: default K=2 (~170ms batched), extend to K=10+CRM when uncertain. [Results TBD]

## Required Subsections (4 subsections)

### 1. VLA Robustness (largest subsection)
**Training-time methods**: SRPO \cite{srpo2025}, RobustVLA \cite{robustvla2025}, DiG-Flow \cite{digflow2025}, TT-VLA \cite{liu2026ttvla}. All require retraining/RL/reward engineering. Cannot serve as drop-in for frozen VLA.

**Inference-time methods**: ReconVLA \cite{chen2026reconvla} (conformal UQ, no correction), SC-VLA \cite{liu2026scvla} (sparse world imagination + residual RL), VLA-Pilot \cite{li2025vlapilot} (evolutionary optimization, 2.41s/step), A2C2 \cite{a2c2_2025} (temporal chunk correction).

**A2C2 positioning** (CRITICAL — closest concurrent work): A2C2 solves temporal staleness (within-chunk correction with new observations). We solve initial action quality (improve the action before execution). They are complementary, not competing. Our pipeline differs: (1) multi-sample selection precedes correction, (2) explicit L2 norm clipping controls magnitude, (3) conditions on observation embedding not temporal features.

### 2. Residual Policy Learning
Silver 2018 \cite{silver2018residual} (foundational residual RL), TRANSIC \cite{jiang2024transic} (learned binary gate — ungated correction → collapse), PLD \cite{xiao2026pld} (bounded ξ via off-policy RL, ICLR 2026), DRC \cite{pan2025drc} (exponential decay). Our approach: fixed L2 norm clipping + supervised L2 loss on demonstration data. No RL, no reward design, no environment interaction.

### 3. Inference-Time Compute Scaling
Snell et al. \cite{snell2024scaling} (LLM test-time compute scaling — selection among candidates is primary mechanism). RoVer \cite{dai2025rover} (reward model as test-time verifier for VLAs — best-of-N with reward scoring). DA-SIP \cite{chun2025dasip} (adaptive denoising steps based on difficulty).

**Key contrast**: In LLM domain, selection/verification is primary mechanism. Our decomposition reveals that in low-dimensional continuous action spaces, learned correction dominates while selection provides centering. This motivates adaptive K allocation (C4): allocate compute based on per-step uncertainty rather than fixed budget.

### 4. Conformal Prediction in Robotics (compressed)
CP for safety/planning: adaptive CBFs \cite{zhou2025acp_cbf}, trajectory optimization \cite{wang2025cploop}, teleoperation calibration \cite{zhao2024conformalized}. We use CP scores as conditioning features for learned correction, finding they do NOT help (Section ablation). This negative result informs C2.

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related_work}

\subsection{VLA Robustness}

VLAs have evolved from tokenized action prediction~\cite{brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla} to generative action models based on diffusion~\cite{chi2023diffusion_policy} and flow matching~\cite{black2024pi0,shukor2025smolvla}, with the latter producing stochastic action samples that enable multi-sample inference.
Robustness evaluations~\cite{fei2025liberoplus} show that state-of-the-art VLAs lose over 65 percentage points under common deployment perturbations, motivating both training-time and inference-time defenses.

\paragraph{Training-time methods.}
SRPO~\cite{srpo2025} applies self-referential RL fine-tuning using the policy's own successful rollouts as reward references.
RobustVLA~\cite{robustvla2025} combines RL post-training with Jacobian regularization to stabilize predictions under observation noise.
DiG-Flow~\cite{digflow2025} gates representation-level control through distributional discrepancy between observation and action embeddings.
TT-VLA~\cite{liu2026ttvla} adapts VLA parameters at test time via RL with progress rewards, but requires per-task reward design and gradient updates during deployment.
These methods require retraining, reward engineering, or per-task RL, and cannot serve as drop-in improvements to a frozen VLA.

\paragraph{Inference-time methods.}
ReconVLA~\cite{chen2026reconvla} applies conformal quantile regression for per-action uncertainty calibration and out-of-distribution detection, but does not learn corrective residuals.
SC-VLA~\cite{liu2026scvla} refines actions through sparse world imagination combined with residual RL, which still requires task-level RL training.
VLA-Pilot~\cite{li2025vlapilot} applies evolutionary diffusion optimization guided by an MLLM verifier at 2.41\,s per control step.
A2C2~\cite{a2c2_2025} learns a lightweight correction head that updates each action within a pre-generated chunk at every control step to restore closed-loop responsiveness.

A2C2 is the closest concurrent work: both attach a learned correction module to a frozen VLA.
The two methods solve different problems: A2C2 corrects \emph{temporal staleness} (chunk actions become outdated as the scene evolves), while our pipeline improves \emph{initial action quality} before execution begins.
Our pipeline additionally differs in three design choices: (1)~multi-sample selection precedes correction, providing a centered starting point, (2)~explicit $L_2$ norm clipping controls correction magnitude (Section~\ref{sec:magnitude_results}), and (3)~the correction module conditions on the frozen VLA's observation embedding rather than temporal action features.

\subsection{Residual Policy Learning}

Residual policy learning augments a base controller with a learned correction~\cite{silver2018residual,johannink2019residual}.
Magnitude control is a central design choice: TRANSIC~\cite{jiang2024transic} gates residuals with a learned binary switch and shows that ungated correction leads to policy collapse, PLD~\cite{xiao2026pld} bounds corrections within $[-\xi, \xi]$ via off-policy RL, and DRC~\cite{pan2025drc} applies exponential decay over the episode.
All three use RL to train the correction policy.
Our pipeline uses fixed $L_2$ norm clipping with supervised loss on demonstration data, requiring no RL, reward design, or environment interaction.
The conditioning-magnitude interaction we study (Section~\ref{sec:magnitude_results}) reveals that the choice of conditioning features can matter more than the magnitude bound itself.

\subsection{Inference-Time Compute Scaling}

Test-time compute scaling improves language model outputs through best-of-N sampling with verifiers~\cite{snell2024scaling} or reward-guided selection~\cite{dai2025rover}.
In embodied control, DA-SIP~\cite{chun2025dasip} adjusts the number of denoising steps per control step based on task difficulty, achieving 2.6--4.4$\times$ compute reduction.
Our $K$-value curve (Section~\ref{sec:main_results}) instantiates test-time scaling for robot action generation, but the decomposition reveals a key difference: in low-dimensional continuous action spaces, learned correction is the active mechanism while selection provides centering, contrasting with the LLM setting where selection among candidates is primary.
This asymmetry motivates adaptive $K$ allocation based on per-step uncertainty rather than fixed-budget sampling (Section~\ref{sec:method}).

\subsection{Conformal Prediction in Robotics}

Conformal prediction provides distribution-free coverage guarantees for robotic safety and planning, including adaptive control barrier functions~\cite{zhou2025acp_cbf}, trajectory optimization~\cite{wang2025cploop}, and teleoperation calibration~\cite{zhao2024conformalized}.
These works use conformal scores as safety constraints.
We instead use conformal statistics as conditioning features for a learned correction module, and find that at $K{=}10$, conformal per-DOF features do not improve over observation-only conditioning and can cause catastrophic failure when the magnitude bound is relaxed (Section~\ref{sec:ablation}).

The question is how to use these samples effectively and when to invest the additional compute.

Recent robustness evaluations~\cite{fei2025liberoplus} show that state-of-the-art VLAs lose over 65 percentage points under common deployment perturbations, making inference-time correction practically relevant.
Training-time methods~\cite{srpo2025,robustvla2025,digflow2025,liu2026ttvla} improve the base policy through robustness-aware objectives or test-time RL, but require retraining and remain bounded by the training distribution.
Inference-time methods leave the policy frozen: ReconVLA~\cite{chen2026reconvla} provides uncertainty quantification but does not learn corrective residuals; A2C2~\cite{a2c2_2025} trains a per-step correction head on action chunks but applies correction unconditionally without multi-sample selection or magnitude control; VLA-Pilot~\cite{li2025vlapilot} applies evolutionary optimization at 2.41\,s per control step.
Despite growing interest, fundamental design questions remain unanswered: how much does selection contribute relative to correction, what features should condition the correction module, how sensitive is performance to correction magnitude, and when should the system invest additional compute at all?

We introduce a sample-select-correct pipeline for inference-time action refinement of frozen flow-matching VLAs.
At each control step, the pipeline draws $K$ action samples from the frozen VLA, selects the candidate closest to the sample mean by $L_2$ distance, and applies a learned residual correction via a lightweight Correction Residual Module (CRM).
The CRM is a ${\sim}$327K-parameter MLP conditioned on the frozen VLA's observation embedding ($\mathbb{R}^{960}$) and the selected action ($\mathbb{R}^{30}$), predicting a residual $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ whose $L_2$ norm is clipped to a bound $\varepsilon$.
The design rests on two principles: correction on a pre-screened starting point is more reliable than correction on an arbitrary single sample, and bounding the correction magnitude prevents compounding errors in closed-loop execution.
The base VLA is never modified; the pipeline attaches as a post-hoc module.

We evaluate on LIBERO-Object and LIBERO-Spatial (10 tasks each) using SmolVLA~\cite{shukor2025smolvla} as the frozen backbone.
On in-distribution tasks, the pipeline at $K{=}10$ achieves $17.6 \pm 2.6$\% (7 seeds) versus $11.3 \pm 1.2$\% for VLA-only on Object ($p = 0.003$, Mann-Whitney U) and $34.3 \pm 1.7$\% versus $29.3 \pm 1.7$\% on Spatial, a consistent $+$5--6\,pp improvement across both benchmarks.

This contrasts with LLM test-time compute scaling~\cite{snell2024scaling}, where selection among candidates is the primary mechanism; in low-dimensional continuous action spaces, the value of repeated sampling lies in providing a centered starting point for learned correction, not in picking winners.
A conditioning study demonstrates that observation features produce robust corrections across all magnitude bounds (14.3--17.6\%), while per-DOF conformal features cause progressive collapse (14\%$\to$0\%) under the same architecture and training.
We identify three distribution shifts that cause the CRM to fail, with a proximity-dependent pattern for task shift: near-OOD (within-suite held-out tasks) produces adversarial degradation ($-$12\,pp), while far-OOD (cross-suite evaluation) yields neutral to mildly positive transfer.
These analytical findings inform the design of an adaptive inference-time compute mechanism: a $K{=}2$ pairwise $L_2$ distance serves as an uncertainty probe ($\rho{=}0.9979$ correlation with $K{=}10$ variance), triggering extended sampling only when the VLA is uncertain.

Multi-sample correction also requires stochastic action diversity absent in tokenized VLAs~\cite{kim2024openvla}.

We propose a sample-select-correct pipeline for frozen flow-matching VLAs that draws multiple action samples, selects the most representative candidate via $L_2$ argmin, and applies a learned residual correction bounded in magnitude.
The Correction Residual Module (CRM) is a ${\sim}$327K-parameter MLP conditioned on the frozen VLA's observation embedding, trained offline on task-specific VLA rollout data.
On in-distribution LIBERO tasks, the pipeline achieves consistent +5--6\,pp improvement across both Object ($17.6 \pm 2.6$\%, 7 seeds, $p = 0.003$) and Spatial ($34.3 \pm 1.7$\%) benchmarks versus the unmodified VLA.
Component decomposition reveals that learned correction is the active mechanism ($+$5.3\,pp at $K{=}10$, 68\% of the gain at $K{=}5$) while multi-sampling is an enabling condition: $K{=}1$ correction falls below baseline (10.3\%), and random selection at $K{=}5$ is harmful.
Observation features produce stable corrections across all magnitude bounds (14.3--17.6\%), while per-DOF conformal features collapse to 0\%.
Three distribution shifts (input, task, feature) form a unified failure framework with a proximity-dependent pattern: near-OOD task shift is adversarial ($-$12\,pp) while far-OOD is neutral.
A $K{=}2$ pairwise $L_2$ distance serves as a cheap uncertainty probe ($\rho{=}0.9979$ vs.\ $K{=}10$ variance), enabling adaptive compute allocation that triggers full correction only when needed.
